claim: Marc Brooker published 'Exponential Backoff And Jitter' on the AWS Architecture Blog on 4 March 2015.
quote: Exponential Backoff And Jitter by Marc Brooker on 04 MAR 2015 in Architecture
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog

claim: Capped exponential backoff without jitter sleeps min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt).
quote: sleep = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Formula is shown as an image (figure 3) in the post; transcribed from the image.

claim: Full Jitter sleeps a uniformly random time between 0 and the capped exponential backoff.
quote: sleep = random_between(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Formula is shown as an image (figure 6); transcribed from the image. The post names it: 'Let's call the algorithm above "Full Jitter"'.

claim: Equal Jitter keeps half the capped backoff and randomizes the other half.
quote: temp = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt) / sleep = temp / 2 + random_between(0, temp / 2)
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Two-line formula shown as an image (figure 10); ' / ' marks the line break. Surrounding text: 'we always keep some of the backoff and jitter by a smaller amount'.

claim: Decorrelated Jitter draws the next sleep uniformly between base and three times the previous sleep, capped.
quote: sleep = min(cap, random_between(base, sleep * 3))
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Formula shown as an image (figure 11); transcribed from the image. A WebFetch summary misreported it as base * 3 ** attempt; the image is authoritative.

claim: The simulation modelled optimistic concurrency control (OCC) clients contending for one row of a remote database over a network with 10 ms mean delay and 4 ms variance; the jitter graph discussion uses 100 contending clients.
quote: the network introduces delay with a mean of 10ms and variance of 4ms.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: The client count is a variable N in the graphs; the post says 'In the case with 100 contending clients, we've reduced our call count by more than half.'

claim: Un-jittered exponential backoff is the worst: more work and more time than every jittered approach.
quote: The no-jitter exponential backoff approach is the clear loser. It not only takes more work, but also takes more time than the jittered approaches.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog

claim: Among jittered schemes Equal Jitter loses; Full Jitter does the least work but takes slightly more time than Decorrelated Jitter, so the choice between those two is not clear-cut.
quote: The "Full Jitter" approach uses less work, but slightly more time. Both approaches, though, present a substantial decrease in client work and server load.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Preceding sentences: 'Of the jittered approaches, "Equal Jitter" is the loser.' and 'The decision between "Decorrelated Jitter" and "Full Jitter" is less clear.' Curly quotes normalised to straight quotes.

claim: With 100 contending clients, adding jitter cut the call count by more than half compared with plain exponential backoff.
quote: In the case with 100 contending clients, we've reduced our call count by more than half.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Curly apostrophe normalised.

claim: A May 2023 update notes the pattern is now built into most AWS SDKs' standard and adaptive retry modes.
quote: Update (May 2023): After 8 years, this solution continues to serve as a pillar for how Amazon builds remote client libraries for resilient systems.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: Continues: 'Most AWS SDKs now support exponential backoff and jitter as part of their retry behavior when using standard or adaptive modes.'

claim: With N clients contending under OCC, total work grows with N squared, and jitter does not change that order.
quote: With N clients contending, the total amount of work done by the system increases with N2.
source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter, Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog
note: N2 is N superscript 2 in the HTML. Later: 'none of these approaches fundamentally change the N2 nature of the work'.

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: Amazon picks a timeout by choosing an acceptable false-timeout rate (for example 0.1%) and using the matching downstream latency percentile (p99.9).
quote: we choose an acceptable rate of false timeouts (such as 0.1%). Then, we look at the corresponding latency percentile on the downstream service (p99.9 in this example).
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library
note: The original URL now 301-redirects to https://builder.aws.com/content/3EumjoZascWd1oZiEgL8ORlv3qE/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter, which renders client-side and returned no article text; text taken from the Wayback Machine copy of the old URL and cross-checked against the official PDF https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter.pdf ('Copyright 2019').

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: The percentile rule fails for clients with large network latency and for services whose p99.9 is close to p50, where padding is needed.
quote: This approach also doesn't work with services that have tight latency bounds, where p99.9 is close to p50. In these cases, adding some padding helps us avoid small latency increases that cause high numbers of timeouts.
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library
note: Curly apostrophe normalised.

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: With a five-deep call stack and three tries at each layer, independent retries multiply the load on the database 243-fold (3^5).
quote: If each layer retries independently, the load on the database will increase 243x, making it unlikely to ever recover.
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library
note: Setup sentence: 'Consider a system where the customer's call causes a five-deep stack of service calls. It ends with a query to a database, and three retries at each layer.' Next: 'the retries at each layer multiply -- first three tries, then nine tries, and so on.' (the '--' appears as-is in the source).

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: Amazon's best practice for low-cost control-plane and data-plane calls is to retry at only one layer of the stack.
quote: In general, for low-cost control-plane and data-plane operations, our best practice is to retry at a single point in the stack.
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: Instead of circuit breakers, Amazon limits retries locally with a token bucket, added to the AWS SDK in 2016.
quote: we can mitigate this risk by limiting retries locally using a token bucket. This allows all calls to retry as long as there are tokens, and then retry at a fixed rate when the tokens are exhausted.
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library
note: Next sentence: 'AWS added this behavior to the AWS SDK in 2016.' The article argues circuit breakers 'introduce modal behavior into systems that can be difficult to test'.

topic: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library)
claim: Retries can worsen overload, so Amazon retries only when the dependency looks healthy and stops when retries are not improving availability.
quote: We avoid this amplification by retrying only when we observe that the dependency is healthy. We stop retrying when the retries are not helping to improve availability.
source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library

claim: AWS SDK standard mode defaults to 3 max attempts (one request plus two retries); DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams default to 4.
quote: A max attempts value of 3 means the SDK makes one initial request and up to two retries. Set max attempts to 1 to disable retries entirely.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
date: not shown (page reflects the May 2026 retry update)
note: Code formatting around 3 and 1 dropped. DynamoDB note: 'The DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams clients default to 4 max attempts.'

claim: The current docs describe a 2026 retry behavior that is opt-in (AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true) until it becomes the default; older SDK behavior differs in backoff timing and quota costs.
quote: Without this setting, your SDK uses pre-2026 retry behavior, which differs in backoff timing, retry quota costs, and service-specific defaults.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
note: Preceding: 'The behavior described on this page requires opting in until it becomes the default behavior. Set AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true in your environment.'

claim: In the 2026 behavior the SDK uses full jitter: delay = random(0,1) x min(20,000 ms, base_delay x 2^retry), with base 50 ms for transient errors and 1,000 ms for throttling errors.
quote: delay = random(0, 1) × min(20,000 ms, base_delay × 2^retry)
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
note: The quote uses the multiplication sign (U+00D7) as in the source. Base delays table: Transient 50 ms, Throttling 1,000 ms; DynamoDB transient base 25 ms.

claim: The maximum backoff cap is 20 seconds, and with the default 3 attempts the cap is never reached.
quote: The maximum backoff cap is 20 seconds. No individual delay exceeds 20 seconds regardless of how many attempts have occurred.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
note: Also: 'With the default of 3 max attempts (1 initial request + 2 retries), the backoff cap is never reached.'

claim: In the 2026 behavior the retry quota holds 500 tokens; a transient retry costs 14, a throttling retry costs 5, a first-try success restores 1.
quote: Budget capacity | 500 tokens | Cost per transient (non-throttling) retry | 14 tokens | Cost per throttling retry | 5 tokens
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
note: Quote is table rows joined with '|'. Also: 'When a request succeeds on the first try (no retries needed), the SDK restores 1 token.' The '5 per retry, 10 per timeout retry' figures in the brief are the PRE-2026 values; see sdk_retry_quota_pre2026.

claim: With 3 max attempts the 2026 quota starts draining when roughly 22% of requests hit sustained transient failures (32% for throttling).
quote: the quota begins to drain when more than approximately 22% of requests result in sustained transient failures, or more than approximately 32% for throttling errors.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide

claim: Before the 2026 update, standard mode (botocore) started with 500 tokens and charged 5 per retry and 10 per timeout retry; the 2026 behavior charges 14 for transient and 5 for throttling retries.
quote: _RETRY_COST = 5 / _RETRY_COST_V2 = 14 / _NO_RETRY_INCREMENT = 1 / _THROTTLING_RETRY_COST = 5 / _TIMEOUT_RETRY_REQUEST = 10
source: botocore/retries/standard.py (RetryQuotaChecker), boto/botocore on GitHub
note: ' / ' separates source lines. Code uses _TIMEOUT_RETRY_REQUEST and _RETRY_COST when NEW_RETRIES_ENABLED is false. INITIAL_CAPACITY = 500 in botocore/retries/quota.py. The AWS announcement (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/announcing-updated-retry-behavior-for-aws-sdks-and-tools/, Matthew Miller, 20 May 2026) says: 'each transient error retry costs 14 tokens (up from 5 in the previous version of standard mode).'

claim: Before 2026 each SDK used one base delay for all error types, varying from 10 ms to 1,000 ms across SDKs.
quote: Previously, each SDK applied the same base delay regardless of error type, but that delay varied across SDKs, from 10 ms to 1,000 ms.
source: Announcing updated retry behavior for AWS SDKs and Tools, Matthew Miller, AWS Developer Tools Blog

claim: Adaptive mode adds a per-client rate limiter that can delay even the first request when throttling is detected, and is not recommended as a general default.
quote: Unlike standard mode, adaptive mode can delay or block the initial request, not just retries, when throttling is detected.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide
note: Also: 'Adaptive mode is not recommended as a general default.'

claim: The pre-2026 SDK reference stated the standard backoff as seconds_to_sleep_i = min(b*r^i, MAX_BACKOFF), with b uniform in [0,1], r = 2 and MAX_BACKOFF 20 seconds for most SDKs.
quote: seconds_to_sleep_i = min(b*r^i, MAX_BACKOFF) In the preceding algorithm, the following values apply: b = random number within the range of: 0 <= b <= 1 r = 2 MAX_BACKOFF = 20 seconds for most SDKs.
source: Retry behavior, AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide (Wayback snapshot 2026-01-01)
note: The live page no longer shows this form; it now shows delay = random(0,1) x min(20,000 ms, base_delay x 2^retry). Also from the snapshot: 'If retry_mode is standard - Makes three attempts.' (en-dash in source replaced by hyphen).

claim: boto3 standard mode defaults to 3 max attempts and backs off by a factor of 2 up to 20 seconds; boto3's legacy mode defaults to 5 attempts.
quote: Any retry attempt will include an exponential backoff by a base factor of 2 for a maximum backoff time of 20 seconds.
source: Retries, Boto3 documentation
note: Also: 'A default value of 3 for maximum attempts (including the initial request).' (standard) and 'A default value of 5 for maximum attempts' (legacy).
